kakekotoba.reading_primary: みをつくし (澪標 - channel marker/buoy)
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: 身を尽くし (to exhaust oneself, give up one's body/life)
kakekotoba.interaction: みをつくし is a kakekotoba spanning ku3-4: 澪標 (channel marker, a wooden post marking navigable water in Naniwa Bay, famous utamakura) is homophonous with 身を尽くし (to exhaust one's body/life, to give everything). The channel-marker image, tied to Naniwa's famous seascape, is invoked purely to license the pivot into 'even if it costs me my life/body, I will meet you.' Both readings are grammatically active: 難波なる (place name modifying) applies literally to the channel-marker reading, while 身をつくしても as a verb phrase applies to the 'exhausting oneself' reading.

kakekotoba.reading_primary: 難波なる (Naniwa, place name, 'that is in Naniwa')
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: 何は・なにはあれ implied 'whatever the case' (weak/associative, not fully independent)
kakekotoba.interaction: Primarily functions as a place-name modifier setting up the みをつくし pivot; included here only as context for the main kakekotoba, not itself a strong independent pivot.

jokotoba.text: 難波なる身をつくして
jokotoba.pivot: みをつくし (澪標/身を尽くし)
jokotoba.function: The Naniwa channel-marker image serves as an extended, poem-specific lead-in (built around the kakekotoba) that motivates and licenses the emotional declaration in the shimo-no-ku; it is not a fixed epithet but composed for this poem's wordplay, functioning jokotoba-like even though its core mechanism is the pivot itself.

honkadori.source_poem: Man'yōshū / traditional Naniwa channel-marker poems (e.g. Man'yōshū anonymous poems using 澪標 imagery of Naniwa Bay)
honkadori.function: Invokes the established poetic association of Naniwa's 澪標 (channel markers) with self-sacrificing devotion, drawing on a long tradition of using this Naniwa utamakura for expressions of romantic determination.

kigo.note: 難波 (Naniwa) is a famous utamakura (poetic place-name) associated with its bay, channel markers, and reeds, but it is not tied to a specific season — it functions here as a place-based rhetorical anchor for the kakekotoba rather than a seasonal marker. No genuine seasonal word is present in this poem; the imagery (channel markers, exhaustion, love) is non-seasonal love poetry (koi no uta).

bipartite.kami_theme: The speaker's present state of despair/resignation ('having grown weary of the world, it is all the same now') set against the Naniwa channel-marker image, establishing both emotional resignation and the wordplay vehicle for what follows.
bipartite.shimo_theme: A resolute declaration: even at the cost of one's own body/life, the speaker will still seek to meet the beloved.
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku voices despair and resignation ('it's all the same now, whatever happens'), which logically should lead to giving up — yet the shimo-no-ku pivots via the みをつくし kakekotoba into a fierce vow of self-sacrificing devotion. The despair of the opening becomes, paradoxically, the very fuel for reckless romantic resolve: because all is already lost, the speaker will now risk everything to meet the beloved, turning resignation into defiant devotion.

source_jp:
わびぬれば
今はた同じ
難波なる
身をつくしても
逢はむとぞ思ふ
